name: Sports
blurb: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance, from NCAA and NFHS governance to Hudl, Catapult, and the sports technology research network.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers arts, entertainment, and recreation in its AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: College sports' governing body is where AI questions about recruiting, roster management, and transfer analytics get policy answers.
points.name: The NCAA governs the college layer

points.desc: The National Federation of State High School Associations monitors scholastic sports tech - safety equipment, automated streaming, and recruiting policy for 12,000+ member schools.
points.name: NFHS covers high school sports technology

points.desc: The Sports & Fitness Industry Association publishes participation and equipment-market research covering technology adoption in youth and scholastic sports.
points.name: SFIA tracks the market data

points.desc: The dominant platform for game film across high school, college, and pro programs - its computer-vision scouting and automated capture cameras are the de facto standard for how AI reaches the sideline.
points.name: Hudl sets the video-analysis standard

points.desc: The primary wearable and tracking platforms for biomechanics and load management in NCAA and professional leagues - where athlete-monitoring AI actually runs.
points.name: Catapult and Kinexon instrument the athletes

points.desc: The Sports Tech Research Network - a nonprofit founded out of Ghent University's sports-innovation consortium - connects academic researchers with industry on sports technology, and published a peer-reviewed quality framework for assessing sports tech.
points.name: STRN bridges the research and the products

summary: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance are the visible deployments. Coverage of who tracks the sector runs from the governing bodies down to the platforms whose tooling sets the de facto standards.

analysis.body:
Arts, entertainment, and recreation firms reported 18.6 percent AI use in the latest Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey, up from 18.2 percent in the prior period, placing the broader sector in a measured but gradually climbing adoption range. Sports sits within that NAICS 71 grouping, so the figure captures the full entertainment and recreation category rather than competitive sports alone, but the trend line is consistent with what the documented vendor activity suggests: adoption is real, incremental, and concentrated in specific functional areas rather than spread evenly across organizations.

The clearest concentration of deployed technology falls in video analysis and athlete monitoring. Hudl operates as the de facto standard for game film across high school, college, and professional programs, using computer vision for scouting and automated camera capture, meaning AI reaches the sideline primarily through a single dominant platform rather than through a fragmented market. Catapult and Kinexon fill the parallel role for on-body data, running the biomechanics and load-management analytics that NCAA programs and professional leagues rely on to manage athlete workload and injury risk. These two functional clusters, video intelligence and wearable tracking, account for where documented vendor activity actually concentrates.

Governance creates a meaningful constraint that distinguishes sports from most other sectors. The NCAA sits as the policy authority for college-level questions about AI in recruiting, roster decisions, and transfer analytics, meaning that even when the technology is technically capable, its permissible use in college sports is subject to a separate regulatory layer that has nothing to do with commercial readiness. The NFHS plays an equivalent role for the roughly 12,000 high school member schools it covers, monitoring how automated streaming and recruiting tools are deployed at the scholastic level. That two-tier governance structure, NCAA above, NFHS below, means compliance review is not optional and varies by competitive level.

For an organization deciding whether to deploy, the practical picture is that the dominant tools are already standardized enough that the vendor selection question is relatively constrained, particularly on the video side where Hudl's market position is documented. The more consequential decisions involve which competitive tier the organization operates in and what the applicable governing body permits, since the technology outpaces the policy in several areas the NCAA and NFHS are still actively addressing. The Sports Tech Research Network has published a peer-reviewed quality framework for evaluating sports technology, which offers a structured starting point for due diligence that goes beyond vendor claims.
